slides.title: Aperitivo is not happy hour.
slides.sub: Same time of day. Completely different religion.

slides.heading: It's about appetite.
paragraphs: The word comes from the Latin aperire — “to open”. It's meant to open your appetite before dinner.
Not to end your evening at 9 p.m.

slides.heading: What to order
items: Prosecco, Aperol or Campari, a splash of soda. Iconic.
Gin, vermouth, Campari. Born in Florence. Not for beginners.
Campari, vermouth, soda. Despite the name, very Italian.

slides.heading: Small bites, big tradition.
paragraphs: Olives, crisps, small sandwiches, cured meats — often included with your drink.
Eat a little. Not everything. This isn't dinner. Unless it's an apericena.

slides.heading: Between 6 and 9 p.m.
paragraphs: Aperitivo usually happens between 6 and 9 p.m. Dinner comes after. Sometimes much after.
The formula: one or two drinks, a lot of conversation, zero hurry.

slides.title: Tag your aperitivo partner.
slides.text: Follow for Italian Rule Nº 7 — and tell us: Spritz or Negroni?

caption:
Italian Rule Nº 6 🍹
Aperitivo is not happy hour.

It's not about cheap drinks. It's about opening your appetite, slowly, with good company and something to nibble. Getting drunk is not on the menu.

Spritz or Negroni? 👇

—
🇮🇹 Regola italiana n.6: l'aperitivo è un rito, non un happy hour. Il vostro drink preferito?
